channel.description: Recent content in MiBeeOSS on Mi&Bee Blog

item.title: MiBeeNvr: From v0.1.0 to v0.10.0
item.description: MiBeeNvr is the NVR I wrote for the cameras in my own home. v0.1.0 shipped on May 6, 2026; v0.10.0-preview landed on July 28 — nine releases in under three months (v0.8 never got its own release post; the problems it exposed became the backbone of v0.9). Each version used to have its own post; this one merges the v0.1.0–v0.10.0 release notes into a single timeline: what each step did, and why.

item.title: MiBeeHive: The "Hive" Toolbox I Built for My Studio
item.description: Coming from an operations background, later transitioning to development, the number of projects I maintain keeps growing. Various middleware, databases, monitoring components… each version upgrade is a manual labor: go to the official site to find the download link, compare version numbers, manually download to the internal network, then distribute to each machine. I used to write a bunch of Shell scripts to periodically pull the latest versions to the LAN — functional but not user-friendly: scripts scattered everywhere, adding new software required writing parsing logic by hand, and there was nothing to check when things went wrong.

item.title: MiBeeSteward: Why I Built Another Device Management Tool in Go
item.description:
As a studio operator, the biggest pain point is never a specific problem — it’s the “not knowing” when devices multiply.

Not knowing which devices are alive, what services are running on them, whether a new machine has appeared on the network, whether a certain port is still open. This accumulated “not knowing” eventually becomes an outage.

My previous approach was a patchwork: Zabbix for monitoring, Nmap for scanning, Excel for asset tracking, Prometheus for metrics. Each tool is fine on its own, but together they’re a disaster — data silos, duplicate configuration, version drift, complex deployment.

item.title: MiBeeNvr's AI Detection: Why Inference Runs in the Browser, and Why YOLO11n
item.description:
MiBeeNvr’s Smart Features include an AI detection option that runs inference entirely in the browser — the backend server does no inference at all. The ONNX model file is served to the browser, and ONNX Runtime Web executes it client-side. The model is Ultralytics’ yolo11n.onnx.

This isn’t a common choice among NVR products. Most open-source NVRs (Frigate, the go2rtc ecosystem) put AI inference on the backend, because the backend has access to the raw stream, runs persistently, and can use a GPU. Moving inference into the browser is a deliberate architectural trade-off, not a stopgap. This post breaks down two things: why inference lives in the browser, and — given that premise — why YOLO11n.

item.title: MiBeeNvr v0.6.0's Test Machines: Three Camera Projects Updated in Sync
item.description: The concurrently released MiBeeNvr v0.6.0 brought major features like timelapse, video transcoding, and ONVIF enhancements. Unit tests alone are far from enough — the full workflow must be tested against real camera hardware. To provide reliable test machines for this release, three camera projects were updated on the same day, June 5th — both to supply testing environments for the NVR and to solve some typical embedded development engineering problems along the way.

item.title: gortmplib vs go2rtc vs FFmpeg: RTMP Push Source Comparison & Integrating with Chinese Live-Streaming Platforms
item.description: To push camera feeds from the MiBee NVR project to a domestic live-streaming platform, there are three candidates: call FFmpeg directly, use the pure-Go gortmplib, or use go2rtc. All three “do RTMP”, but their behaviour against Chinese live-streaming platforms differs wildly — some disconnect instantly, some after a few seconds, some are rock solid. This post tears all three apart at the source level, and walks through the pitfalls and fixes for integrating with FMS-compatible domestic platforms.

item.title: MiBeeSteward v0.2.0: Distributed Discovery and Change Detection
item.description:
When v0.1.0 shipped, I wrote that it answers three questions: what devices are on the network, what they are, and how they relate. Honestly, v0.1.0 only answered the first half well — and only for the one LAN the center sat on.

The real-world layout is messier: one subnet in the office, one in the server room, another at home for test machines. The center lives in the office and literally cannot see the cameras in the server room. Getting it to scan the server room means crossing subnets — either opening up SNMP routing or just moving the center over there. Neither is elegant.

item.title: MiBeeSteward v0.2.0 Internals: Anti-Entropy and Change Detection
item.description:
The previous post covered what v0.2.0 ships. This one covers why it’s designed that way — distributed consistency is the heaviest part of this release, and several seemingly casual decisions have specific trade-offs behind them.

The problem is clear: the center can only see its own LAN, but users have several. Dropping a center into every subnet isn’t realistic, so enter mibee-agent — a binary that only “scans local + reports to center.” But the moment an agent exists, it drags along a whole string of protocol questions: how to report, how to reconcile, how to detect offline, how not to overwhelm the center’s writes. Let’s take them one at a time.

item.title: MiBeeSteward v0.3.0: Topology, Certificates, and Containers
item.description:
Take over an unfamiliar LAN and the first thing you need is to figure out what’s on it — office, server room, and home subnets tangled together, no documentation left behind, a switch full of MACs nobody can name. MiBeeSteward exists for exactly that: scan the network and tell you what devices are there, what they are, and how they connect.

v0.3.0 goes after three specific pains left over from the last two releases:

item.title: MiBeeSteward v0.3.0 Internals: Probe Fidelity and Certificate Chains
item.description:
The previous post covered what v0.3.0 ships. This one covers why — this release has three seemingly casual decisions with specific engineering trade-offs behind them: how the Docker network mode decides the scanner’s probe fidelity, why TLS cert-chain collection can cover eight protocols with one core, and why L2 topology needs three MIBs to assemble. Let’s take them one at a time.

Docker Network Mode vs Probe Fidelity

item.title: MiBeeNvr v0.11.0: fnOS Installs, GB/T 28181, and the Full-Day Timeline
item.description:
A few days after v0.10.0 went stable, fnOS users’ feedback boiled down to one sentence: it won’t install. Two older debts got settled in the same release: Hikvision/Dahua cameras couldn’t enroll — you either bought their NVR or stood up a separate GB platform; and playback showed one 30-second segment at a time, so reviewing a whole day meant clicking through segment by segment.

It installs now

  • All three install blockers are fixed: stalling on image downloads, a dead desktop icon, and a port field that rejected 9090 outright
  • The offline package bundles the full image set — works the moment it’s installed, no network needed
  • The online package is a few dozen KB and picks whichever of the China mirror or the official registry answers faster
  • The one-click install script auto-selects the same way
  • Synology, QNAP, and ZSpace store templates landed too

Easier to integrate

  • Hikvision/Dahua cameras enroll with a few filled-in fields — no vendor NVR, no separate platform (via the GB/T 28181 national standard)
  • Fully automatic after registration: a camera card per channel, recording starts on its own
  • PTZ, zoom, presets, and voice intercom work; the recordings on the camera’s own SD card are searchable and replayable
  • Hand Home Assistant-style integrations a dedicated key you can revoke on its own, without touching the global password
  • An IP change no longer breaks clients — they track the device, not the address

Playback that works

  • A whole day’s recordings stitch into one timeline — scrub to any moment
  • Segment switches no longer black-flash; the handover is invisible
  • Blank stretches from power cuts scrub right through without stalling
  • Authenticated live streams play on iPhone again

If it doesn’t install, it isn’t released.

item.title: MiBeeSteward v0.4.0: Discovery on the Router Itself
item.description:
Finding out what lives on your LAN used to mean active scanning — traffic, blind spots — or running in a container, which needed host networking just to see the full device table. Meanwhile the router knows everything already, and the discovery system was walking around it.

Live on the router, everything visible

  • The discovery program runs on the router itself: who joined the WiFi, who got which IP, who is online right now — the router already knows, so it just reads
  • No port scanning, no probe traffic; the full device list appears quietly
  • OpenWrt installs and runs as a first-class citizen

A more trustworthy device ledger

  • A device changing IP no longer forks into “old and new” phantom entries
  • One authoritative record per device; history stops diverging

The gateway already knows everything — just ask it.

item.title: MiBeeSteward v0.5.0: Three Things for the Enterprise
item.description: Bringing an internal-network device manager into a company — or any stricter environment — runs into three walls: SNMP stopped at v2c, with cleartext community strings riding the wire that no security audit passes and many hardened networks simply disable, paralyzing collection outright; permissions came in just two tiers, admin and user, so shared deployments couldn’t separate who operates from who merely looks; and the first question of a network postmortem — “when was this config changed, and by whom” — had no answer.

item.title: Where Should MiBeeSteward Live: Router Form vs Host Form, a Controlled Comparison
item.description: MiBee Steward is an open-source network device management system (a single Go binary handling automatic discovery, identification, and the ledger of LAN devices) with three deployment shapes: directly on the router, on an ordinary host in the network, or one center with several lightweight agents covering multiple subnets. This time, on one physical network, all three shapes were compared under the same version and parameters — environment, process, and data laid out to answer “where should it live”.

item.title: Taking Over onvif-go: Real-Camera Fixes, Zero Dependencies, and Service Facades
item.description:
MiBeeNvr talks to cameras over ONVIF, and this library is what sits underneath. ONVIF is the de facto standard for IP video surveillance equipment: device discovery, media profiles, PTZ control, event subscriptions — all one set of SOAP-over-HTTP service conventions. Any brand that claims ONVIF compliance can, in theory, be integrated through the same calls.

onvif-go is that stack implemented in Go. We did not write it from scratch: its upstream was 0x524a/onvif-go — the previous author reshaped it into its modern form of a client plus a virtual camera server (the git history still traces back to earlier Go ONVIF attempts in the community). But upstream stalled entering 2026: the last merged PR landed in mid-January, the v1.0-through-v1.1.3 release cadence from late 2025 never resumed, and three Improve Test Coverage issues filed in November 2025 sit unclaimed to this day. Meanwhile we hit two problems in our own camera pool that could only be fixed inside the library.

item.title: Four Protocol Libraries, Extracted: ONVIF and GB28181 in Go and Rust
item.description:
MiBee’s camera access runs on two protocols. ONVIF is the de facto standard internationally — Hikvision, Axis, Dahua, and Bosch all speak it. GB/T 28181 is China’s national surveillance standard, unavoidable in government and state-owned projects. The device side (Raspberry Pi camera firmware, one Go and one Rust implementation) and the NVR side (MiBeeNvr, Go) both speak these two protocols, and the stacks have always lived inside the projects.

Two problems with that. First, this code is pickled in interop details — digest-auth qop handling, SIP Via-branch uniqueness, MANSCDP element-vs-attribute dual forms, TCP framing header byte counts — each one was ground out against a real platform, and a new project would have to grind them all again. Second, a library survey two weeks ago showed the open-source landscape for these protocols is unevenly populated; several positions have no one standing in them.

item.title: MiBeeNvr v0.12.0: Sub-streams, Adaptive Recording, and Full-path Observability
item.description:
MiBeeNvr v0.12.0 is out. This release goes after two everyday annoyances: watching the cameras on a phone, where a thumbnail-sized preview quietly pulls the full-resolution video underneath — eating data and heating the phone; and corridor or doorway cameras writing tens of GB a day that nobody ever replays.

Less disk

  • When nothing moves, the camera records less; the moment anything moves, it snaps back to full recording without dropping a frame. Quiet scenes measured at roughly 3/4 less disk
  • A louder sound, a doorbell, or a sensor signal also kicks it back to full recording
  • The replay timeline carries a green-to-red heat strip — the segments where something happened are visible at a glance
  • When the disk nears full, the quietest recordings are deleted first
  • Phone viewing defaults to a small, smooth stream: no stutter, no heat; one tap switches to HD for detail
  • When nobody is watching, that preview stream disconnects by itself — no camera connection or bandwidth tied up

item.title: Hugo Blog SEO: A Complete Guide from Principles to Practice
item.description: It doesn’t matter how good your content is — if search engines can’t crawl it and users can’t find it, it might as well not exist. That sounds harsh, but for the vast majority of independent blogs it’s simply the truth. Your server sits on some VPS, your domain has little authority, backlinks are scarce, and Googlebot might swing by only once a month — and every time it does, it sees the same content from weeks ago. The keywords readers type into the search box will never point to your pages. A painstakingly polished technical article ends up gathering dust in your own archive page.

item.title: Zhi Theme v0.2.0: Language Switcher + Post Series + Mermaid Upgrade
item.description:
This blog has been bilingual from the start, but readers had no way to switch languages; and topic series spanning categories (a seven-post run scattered across two categories, say) couldn’t be read in order.

Language, one tap away

  • A globe button in the header opens every translation of the current page
  • Switching stays on the article — no bouncing back to the homepage
  • Hidden automatically on single-language sites; keyboard-accessible

Series you can read in order

  • Cross-category topics get their own series pages: card-layout overview, timeline-layout detail
  • Ascending/descending order with one tap

Diagrams on the new version

  • Mermaid moves to v11+, with automatic dark-mode adaptation

Your own blog should work for yourself first.

item.title: One Month with the Zhi Theme: Mermaid v11 Upgrade Experience
item.description:
One Month In

It’s been nearly a month since the previous article Switched My Blog Theme: From Hugo NexT to Self-Written Zhi. During this month, the theme has been running stably without major issues. Replacing the NexT theme was the right decision — although there was some initial adjustment, the experience is now significantly better.

After a month of use, the theme’s stability has exceeded expectations. My initial concerns — whether pure Hugo Pipes without build tools could support complex requirements — were proven unfounded. Daily maintenance has become very simple; modifying a feature no longer requires digging through deeply nested SCSS files — one CSS file gets the job done.

item.title: Switched My Blog Theme: From Hugo NexT to Self-Written Zhi
item.description:
Why Switch

This blog previously used Hugo NexT, forked for custom modifications. NexT itself is a feature-rich theme, but when it comes to “customizing things yourself,” the experience wasn’t great.

The issues boiled down to a few things:

SCSS nesting hell. 101 SCSS files, three levels of directory nesting. _common/components/post, _common/components/third-party, _common/outline/sidebar… To change a style, you first had to figure out which file it was in, where variables were defined, and which scheme was overriding it. Not that it couldn’t be done, but each change meant half an hour of hunting.
